newsitem.title: JAPAN: Cautious mood to hang over Tokyo stocks.
newsitem.headline: Cautious mood to hang over Tokyo stocks.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market is expected to be engulfed in a cautious mood in the coming week as investors navigate their way through a week loaded with potential land mines, brokers said.

Brokers said they expect the 225-share Nikkei average to end the 1996/97 business year on March 31 within the 18,000 to 18,500 range, much in line with expectations. In the previous year, the benchmark finished at 21,406.85.

"There are worries about a decrease in unrealised profits of stocks held by firms, but as long as the index is within the range, a meltdown of the financial system, which is what the market is really paranoid of, can be avoided," a fund manager at a foreign investment advisory firm said.
Nikko Securities Co Ltd said warning bells of serious trouble in the financial sector would start to sound if the Nikkei average were to fall to 15,000.
Brokers said the market was waiting for the government to unveil plans to energise the stagnant property market, which would help financial institutions get rid of their bad loans.
The plans, which will be revealed on Monday will provide support to stocks, but are unlikely to send them soaring, they said.
"If they (plans) were earth-shattering, the government wouldn't wait until the last minute to announce them," a "Big Four" broker said.
Although the old year is seen ending without much of a fuss, market sources said the following days could be volatile and investors could opt for the sidelines.

"The new year and the consumption tax rise starts on Tuesday, the Bank of Japan "tankan" survey is due out Wednesday and the U.S. payroll data is due out Friday," Seiki Orimi, Dai-Ichi Securities analyst, said. "Too many items to watch out for."
Brokers said there was a chance the new year could start out on a negative tone, as profit-taking could emerge.
But others said that as shares in the financial sector had declined somewhat in the past week and window dressing was not as active as in the past, there should not be a plunge.

Such uncertainties, and also those concerning the possibility of an economic slowdown after the sales tax is raised and the ending of special tax cuts, were the largest burden on the market, brokers said.
"The market may not be as gloomy as it seems," Keiko Kondo, Merrill Lynch Japan strategist said.
Kondo said with the U.S. stock market showing signs of turbulence, attention could turn to the Japanese market.

"Certain sectors (such as financials) are weak and have the potential to pull down the indices, but there are still other sectors and issues which are attractive which can be picked up at bargain prices," she added.
Besides the foreign investors, pension funds could step up their buying in the new year, Dai-Ichi's Orimi said.
On Friday, the Nikkei average finished down 20.70 points or 0.11 percent at 18,189.72. The index was down nearly 450 points from the previous Friday.
